tagline: Mobile-first video editor with templates, captions, and effects.
verdictSummary: A captioning-and-clipping CLI — transcribe, burn captions, trim, export for social formats — is a real one-sitting build on open-source tools, running fully offline after the model downloads once. What doesn't come with it is CapCut's actual product: a full mobile timeline editor, its effects and template library, and the polish that makes editing fast on a phone.
coreLoopDIY: A command-line tool that transcribes a video locally, burns in styled captions, trims clips, and exports for common social aspect ratios.
whyPeopleStillPay: Short-form editing on a phone needs to be fast, and a library of reusable effects and trends is most of what makes a clip feel current — neither is something a captioning script replicates.
notes: A good category to be honest about: automatic captions are a solved problem; a real timeline editor with effects is not.
prompt:
Build a command-line video captioning and clipping tool. Given a video file, transcribe it locally (faster-whisper or whisper.cpp — no cloud API needed) and burn in styled captions grouped a few words per line, with a config file controlling font, size, color, and position. Support trimming to a time range and exporting at common social aspect ratios (vertical, square, widescreen) with sensible default bitrates for phone playback. Write the plain subtitle file alongside the video so typos can be fixed by hand, then re-burn from the corrected file without re-transcribing. Never overwrite the source file — always write a new output file next to it. Support batch mode: point it at a folder and process every video inside.

Do not build a timeline editor, an effects or template library, or a music library — CapCut's editing polish and asset library are the actual product, and this tool is scoped to one specific job: captioned, trimmed, correctly-sized clips from a single source video, not general editing.

faq.q: Can I import my existing CapCut projects?
faq.a: No — CapCut's project format is proprietary and doesn't export to anything this tool can read. You'd start from the exported video file, not the editable project.

faq.q: Will it work on my phone?
faq.a: No — this is a command-line tool meant to run on a computer with real processing power for transcription. CapCut's mobile-first editing is exactly the part this doesn't replace.

faq.q: What does it cost to run?
faq.a: Nothing — it runs fully offline on your own machine after the one-time transcription model download, with no hosting and no API key.

faq.q: What's the one thing that doesn't survive the rebuild?
faq.a: The editor itself. This tool captions and trims a single clip; it has no timeline, no drag-and-drop effects, and no library of trending templates — for anything beyond captions and a trim, you're back to a real video editor.

faq.q: What's the best free CapCut alternative?
faq.a: Kdenlive is the best fit if you want a full free editor on a laptop: it is multi-platform, has hundreds of effects, animates them with keyframes and transcribes subtitles automatically. Shotcut is the alternative with FFmpeg-wide format support. Neither has CapCut's templates or phone editing.

faq.q: Do these editors need an account or a subscription?
faq.a: No. They run locally on your computer. Flowblade states there is no account, subscription or export fee, and Shotcut and Kdenlive are desktop programs with no cloud storage or shared workspace. Your projects stay as files on your disk.

alternativesIntro: The best free CapCut alternative is Kdenlive: a multi-track desktop editor for Linux, Windows, macOS and BSD with hundreds of effects, keyframe animation and automatic subtitle transcription. It has no template library, no bundled stock media and no phone app, so you lose the quick short-video workflow CapCut is built for. Shotcut is the other solid pick, using FFmpeg for wide format support. OpenCut targets web, desktop and mobile, but its main repository is mid-rewrite today. A small clipping and social-export tool is a one-sitting build. Keep paying if you edit on your phone every day.

alternativeNotes.kdenlive: Covers multi-track editing, keyframed effects, automatic subtitle transcription and local rendering. It has no stock footage, music or templates, and no cloud sync.
alternativeNotes.shotcut: Covers timeline editing with FFmpeg formats and Frei0r and MLT filters on all three desktop systems. It has no template library and no one-tap short-video tools.
alternativeNotes.openshot: Covers unlimited tracks, keyframe animation, chroma key and title templates. It is desktop only, and hardware encoding is labelled experimental.
alternativeNotes.opencut: Aims to be a free MIT editor for web, desktop and mobile. The main repository is a rewrite in progress, so follow it rather than depend on it.
alternativeNotes.flowblade: Covers a multitrack timeline with keyframed compositing and many filters. It runs on Linux only, with no templates, stock media or automatic captions described.
